title: Many-Shot In-Context Jailbreak Dose-Response Tool

original_idea.body:
# Many-Shot In-Context Jailbreak Dose-Response Tool

**Problem:** Long-context models enable many-shot jailbreaking (stuffing many harmful Q&A examples into context), but there is no compact tool that maps attack success against the NUMBER of in-context demonstrations for open long-context models.

**Direction:** Construct a fixed pool of harmful demonstration pairs and prepend k of them (k = 1,2,4,...,128, context-permitting) before a held-out harmful query, measuring ASR as a function of k for open long-context models. Output a 'many-shot dose-response curve' and the k where each model breaks. Ship the harness.

**Why it matters:** Many-shot jailbreaking scales with context length, a growing medium-horizon threat as context windows expand; a dose-response tool quantifies the exposure per model. (Catalogue covered 'dose-response curves for harmful capability elicitation' generally; this is a distinct context-length axis.) Inference-only, single GPU with a modest-context open model.

**Relevant context:** Many-shot jailbreaking (Anthropic 2024) shows ASR rises with number of in-context harmful demonstrations, exploiting long context. StrongREJECT (arXiv:2402.10260) provides the harmful queries and evaluator.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped single experiment (sweep k, plot ASR) with a well-defined deliverable and success criteria.

title: Decoding Randomness x Overseer Determinism: Sampling Variance Defeats Single-Pass Review

original_idea.body:
# Decoding Randomness x Overseer Determinism: Sampling Variance Defeats Single-Pass Review

**Problem:** Two failure modes compound: (A) output variance across decoding (a model produces safe and unsafe completions for the same prompt depending on sampling) and (B) single-pass oversight (a judge reviews one sampled output). A single review can pass a prompt that is unsafe under a large fraction of samples, so oversight reliability is overstated by single-shot evaluation.

**Direction:** For a set of borderline prompts, sample many completions per prompt from an open model at realistic temperature. Have an open judge flag each. Measure the gap between 'unsafe under at least one sample' and 'unsafe under the single sample an overseer happened to review.' The compounding metric is the under-detection of single-pass oversight relative to the true per-prompt unsafe probability.

**Why it matters:** Oversight is usually applied to a single output; deployment serves many stochastic samples. Quantifying how much single-pass review understates true unsafe-rate argues for sampling-aware oversight. Builds on but extends 'consistency across decoding parameters' by tying variance directly to oversight miss-rate. Inference + counting.

**Relevant context:** Catalogue has 'Consistency of Safety Across Decoding Parameters'; this composes decoding variance with the oversight detection gap, a distinct compounding framing. Weak-to-strong safety pilot (arXiv 2410.12621) on overseer miss-rates.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain (quantify single-pass under-detection -> sampling-aware oversight) but the link to catastrophic risk is somewhat indirect.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Accessible: sampling completions + an open judge, counting; standard tools, no training.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped: sample-many, judge each, compute the detection gap; clear success metric.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Independent-friendly oversight-reliability measurement using public models; weak lab incentive.

low_compute.reasoning: Inference + many samples on an open model; single mid GPU.

novelty.reasoning: Decoding-variance and oversight studied separately; this specific compounding metric may be open.

novelty_assessment.reasoning: Component effects known; the variance-x-oversight-gap composition may be open.

title: Rubric Self-Preference x Reward Hacking: Structured Scoring Doesn't Save You

original_idea.body:
# Rubric Self-Preference x Reward Hacking: Structured Scoring Doesn't Save You

**Problem:** Two failure modes compound: (A) self-preference bias surviving rubric-based scoring (judges still favor own-style outputs even with explicit rubrics) and (B) reward hacking (generators optimize to the judge). Rubrics are sold as a debiasing fix; if self-preference leaks through rubric scoring, the generator can still hack the supposedly objective signal.

**Direction:** Score a fixed answer set with an open judge using (1) free-form scoring and (2) detailed rubric scoring, comparing in-family vs out-of-family generations of matched quality. Measure whether the self-preference gap shrinks under rubrics. Then test whether a cheap style edit still moves rubric scores. The compounding metric: residual hackability that survives rubric structure.

**Why it matters:** Rubrics are the standard recommended mitigation for judge bias (and the project requires rubrics for any numeric score). Empirically showing rubrics fail to remove self-preference — and that hacking persists — tempers a widely-trusted oversight safeguard. Inference + comparison; clean 30h project.

**Relevant context:** Self-Preference Bias in Rubric-Based Evaluation of LLMs (arXiv 2604.06996) finds self-preference persists under rubrics. UDA debiasing (arXiv 2508.09724). One Token to Fool LLM-as-a-Judge (arXiv 2507.08794).

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: rubrics are a trusted oversight safeguard; showing residual self-preference/hackability directly tempers reliance on a widely-used mitigation.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Accessible: free-form vs rubric scoring comparison with open judges, inference-only.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped: two scoring conditions, in/out-family pairs, a style-edit hack test; clear metrics.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Independent-friendly third-party scrutiny of a recommended safeguard with public models.

low_compute.reasoning: Inference + comparison on an open judge; single mid GPU.

novelty.reasoning: Self-preference-under-rubrics is published (2604.06996); the compounded hackability angle may be partly open.

novelty_assessment.reasoning: Base finding published; the rubric-survival-plus-hacking composition may be open.

title: Translation Laundering x Oversight: Cross-Lingual Round-Trip Evades Safety Review

original_idea.body:
# Translation Laundering x Oversight: Cross-Lingual Round-Trip Evades Safety Review

**Problem:** Two failure modes compound: (A) cross-lingual safety inconsistency (safety behavior differs across languages) and (B) oversight applied in one language. An unsafe request laundered through translation may be approved by an overseer reviewing the translated (possibly softened or misrendered) version, then re-translated to recover the harmful content.

**Direction:** Take unsafe requests, translate to a pivot language with an open MT model, have an open judge review the pivot-language version, then translate the (possibly approved) response back. Measure how often round-trip translation flips an overseer's verdict from unsafe to safe. The compounding metric is the laundering success rate created by stacking translation distortion onto monolingual oversight.

**Why it matters:** This is a concrete, attacker-relevant compounding pathway for global deployments that frontier labs under-resource for non-English oversight. It studies a long-horizon, diffuse threat with no lab infrastructure — just open MT + an open judge. High counterfactual value.

**Relevant context:** Weak-to-strong safety pilot (arXiv 2410.12621) on overseer failures; cross-lingual safety gaps established. Distinct from catalogue's static cross-lingual mapping by adding the round-trip oversight-evasion mechanism.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: a concrete attacker-relevant laundering pathway for under-resourced non-English oversight, with a defensible safety scenario.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Accessible: open MT + open judge, translate-judge-retranslate, inference-only.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped single experiment with a clear laundering-success-rate metric.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Independent-friendly: labs under-resource non-English oversight; needs no internal access.

title: Anchoring on the First Debater x Order Manipulation: Protocol-Level Position Bias

original_idea.body:
# Anchoring on the First Debater x Order Manipulation: Protocol-Level Position Bias

**Problem:** Two failure modes compound: (A) judge position/anchoring bias and (B) debate-protocol structure that fixes a turn order. If judges anchor on whichever debater speaks first, an adversary who can control or predict speaking order gains an advantage independent of argument quality — a protocol-level vulnerability where a generic judge bias becomes a debate exploit.

**Direction:** Run debates on a QA set under both turn orders (truth-teller first vs deceiver first) with an open judge. Measure how much the judge's verdict depends on order rather than correctness, and whether 'always speak first' is a reliable winning strategy for the wrong side. The compounding metric is the win-rate swing attributable purely to order in the debate setting.

**Why it matters:** Position bias is studied in pairwise judging but rarely in multi-turn debate, where order is a manipulable lever. If oversight-via-debate is order-sensitive, the protocol needs order randomization/balancing as a hard requirement. Inference + win-rate analysis on open models.

**Relevant context:** Position bias documented in LLM judges (arXiv 2603.08091). Kenton et al. (NeurIPS 2024) weak-judges debate setup. A Benchmark for Scalable Oversight Protocols (arXiv 2504.03731).

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: order-sensitivity of debate oversight implies a concrete protocol requirement (order randomization); link to oversight reliability is explicit.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Accessible: run debates both orders with an open judge, win-rate analysis; inference-only.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped: two turn orders, measure order-attributable swing; clear metric.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Independent-friendly debate-protocol scrutiny with public models; weak lab incentive.

low_compute.reasoning: Inference-only multi-turn debates; single mid GPU.

title: Weak Overseer x Tool-Augmented Generator: Oversight Can't Check the Tools

original_idea.body:
# Weak Overseer x Tool-Augmented Generator: Oversight Can't Check the Tools

**Problem:** Two failure modes compound: (A) weak-to-strong oversight gap and (B) tool-augmented generation (the model's answer depends on tool calls/retrieved content the overseer cannot or does not verify). The overseer judges the final text but cannot validate the tool steps, so a generator can justify a wrong answer with fabricated tool outputs the weak overseer accepts at face value.

**Direction:** Give an open generator a QA task where it cites a (simulated) tool/retrieval result, sometimes fabricated. Have an open judge that sees only the final answer + cited evidence rate correctness. Measure how often fabricated-but-plausible evidence gets the wrong answer approved. The compounding metric: approval lift from unverifiable tool citations on top of baseline overseer error.

**Why it matters:** Real oversight of agentic systems must cover tool use, but text-only overseers cannot. Showing that unverifiable evidence systematically inflates approval argues that scalable oversight of agents needs tool-trace verification, not just output review. Prompt-based simulation; light compute; agent-monitoring infrastructure relevance.

**Relevant context:** Kenton et al. (NeurIPS 2024): eloquent/hallucinatory evidence misleads weak judges. EvilGenie (arXiv 2511.21654) on verifier manipulation. Weak-to-strong safety pilot (arXiv 2410.12621).

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: shows text-only oversight of agents is fooled by unverifiable tool evidence, arguing for tool-trace verification; concrete agentic-deployment scenario.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Accessible: prompt-based simulation of cited tool outputs, open judge; light compute.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped: fabricated-vs-real cited evidence, measure approval lift; clear metric.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Independent-friendly agent-monitoring infrastructure relevance with public models.

low_compute.reasoning: Prompt-based simulation, mostly inference; can run on a small open model.

novelty.reasoning: Eloquent-evidence-misleads-judges shown (Kenton); the fabricated-tool-citation oversight angle may be open.

novelty_assessment.reasoning: Related judge-deception results exist; the tool-citation compounding angle may be open.

title: Does a Single Critique Beat Debate Outside Verifiable Domains?

original_idea.body:
# Does a Single Critique Beat Debate Outside Verifiable Domains?

**Problem:** Debate Helps Weak Judges Reward Stronger Models (arXiv:2605.27483, May 2026) shows that on programmatically verifiable code/logic tasks, a single independent critique recovers most of debate's benefit at lower cost. But it is unknown whether this holds for fuzzy, non-verifiable judgments where there is no ground-truth checker — exactly the regime where scalable oversight is hardest.

**Direction:** Reuse the paper's answer-critique-judge primitive but apply it to a non-verifiable task suite (e.g., summarization faithfulness, ethical reasoning, or open-ended QA) where a weak open model (e.g., Llama-3 8B) judges a stronger model's (e.g., 70B via API) answers. Compare three conditions on the same items: bare judge, judge+single-critique, judge+two-round debate. Measure judge accuracy against held-out human/gold labels and whether the single-critique advantage survives without a verifier.

**Why it matters:** If the cheap single-critique primitive only works when a ground-truth checker exists, labs may over-generalize a result that fails precisely in the diffuse-reward regime that matters most for long-horizon oversight. A clean negative or boundary result is high counterfactual value and needs no training.

**Relevant context:** Debate Helps Weak Judges Reward Stronger Models (arXiv:2605.27483, ~May 2026): ablating rebuttal rounds produces no measurable change in judge performance; a single independent critique recovers the bulk of debate's benefit at lower inference cost; results obtained on programmatically verifiable code and logic tasks.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: tests whether a key oversight result transfers to the non-verifiable regime that matters most for long-horizon oversight; clear implication.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Guided: clear inherited answer-critique-judge methodology; weak-judge/strong-model setup executable by novice+mentor.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped: three conditions on one task suite, accuracy vs gold; clear success criteria.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Independent-friendly boundary/negative result on public models; high counterfactual value.

low_compute.reasoning: Inference, possibly a 70B via API; single GPU plus API.

novelty.reasoning: Direct extension of a very recent (May 2026) paper to the untested non-verifiable regime; likely no published work.

novelty_assessment.reasoning: Extends a May-2026 result to an explicitly untested regime; likely no direct published work.

title: Critique Helpfulness vs. Judge Gullibility: Disentangling Why Critiques Help

original_idea.body:
# Critique Helpfulness vs. Judge Gullibility: Disentangling Why Critiques Help

**Problem:** The same May 2026 paper finds debate/critique helps 'when the critic provides a usable advantage,' but does not separate whether gains come from genuinely informative critiques versus the judge simply deferring to any confident critique. These are very different oversight stories.

**Direction:** Run the answer-critique-judge protocol but inject controlled adversarial critiques: (a) correct critiques, (b) plausible-but-wrong critiques, (c) content-free confident critiques. Measure how often the weak judge flips its verdict in each condition on verifiable tasks. A judge that flips equally for wrong/empty critiques is being persuaded, not informed.

**Why it matters:** Distinguishing 'informed deference' from 'persuasion-driven deference' is central to whether critique-based oversight is robust to a strategic model that produces confident misleading critiques. Pure prompting study, single GPU.

**Relevant context:** Debate Helps Weak Judges Reward Stronger Models (arXiv:2605.27483, ~May 2026): debate helps the judge over a consultancy baseline only when the critic provides a usable advantage. Related sycophancy findings in Measuring Opinion Bias and Sycophancy via LLM-based Persuasion (arXiv:2604.21564) report sycophancy up to 94% under indirect/argumentative probing.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: separating informed vs persuasion-driven deference is central to whether critique-oversight is robust to a strategic misleader.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Accessible: pure prompting with three controlled critique conditions; single GPU.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped: three injected-critique conditions, measure flip rate; clear metric.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Independent-friendly mechanism study on public models; weak lab incentive.

low_compute.reasoning: Pure prompting study; runs on a small open model.

title: When Does Knowledge Divergence Make Debate Worthless? A Replication Sweep

original_idea.body:
# When Does Knowledge Divergence Make Debate Worthless? A Replication Sweep

**Problem:** Knowledge Divergence and the Value of Debate for Scalable Oversight (arXiv:2603.05293, Mar 2026) argues debate's value depends on the gap between what debaters and judges know. The practical breakpoint — how much knowledge divergence kills debate's benefit — is underexplored on cheap open models.

**Direction:** Operationalize knowledge divergence by controlling what information the judge model is given (full context, partial context, no context) on a QA dataset, holding debaters fixed. Plot judge accuracy gain from debate vs. the size of the judge's information deficit. Identify the divergence threshold where debate stops helping or starts hurting.

**Why it matters:** Real oversight is the high-divergence regime (weak overseer, capable model). Empirically mapping where debate breaks down is exactly the 'formal-ish guarantees / impossibility boundary' open problem, done cheaply with prompting only.

**Relevant context:** Knowledge Divergence and the Value of Debate for Scalable Oversight (arXiv:2603.05293, Mar 2026): the value of debate for oversight is tied to the divergence between debater and judge knowledge. Builds on On scalable oversight with weak LLMs judging strong LLMs (arXiv:2407.04622).

title: Do Bias-Mitigation Prompts Actually Mitigate, or Just Move the Bias?

original_idea.body:
# Do Bias-Mitigation Prompts Actually Mitigate, or Just Move the Bias?

**Problem:** Judging the Judges (arXiv:2604.23178, Apr 2026) evaluates bias-mitigation strategies for LLM judges but the field assumes mitigations are additive and side-effect-free. A mitigation that reduces position bias might inflate verbosity bias.

**Direction:** Take 2-3 published mitigation prompts and measure their effect on a panel of biases simultaneously (position, verbosity, authority) rather than the single bias each targets. Construct a bias-interaction matrix showing where fixing one bias worsens another.

**Why it matters:** Oversight pipelines stack mitigations; if they trade off, the net reliability gain is illusory. This is a cheap, high-leverage check that labs rarely run because they optimize one metric at a time.

**Relevant context:** Judging the Judges: A Systematic Evaluation of Bias Mitigation Strategies in LLM-as-a-Judge Pipelines (arXiv:2604.23178, Apr 2026): LLM judges exhibit systematic biases that compromise evaluation reliability; the paper compares mitigation strategies. title: Harmful-Continuation 'Point of No Return' Benchmark

original_idea.body:
# Harmful-Continuation 'Point of No Return' Benchmark

**Problem:** Following shallow alignment, a useful unmeasured property is how RECOVERABLE a model is mid-generation: if forced to begin a harmful answer, at what response length does it stop being able to self-correct back into a refusal? No benchmark measures this recovery capacity.

**Direction:** Prefill open models with increasingly long harmful continuations (k harmful tokens) and measure the rate at which the model self-corrects (pivots to a refusal/safe redirection) vs continues harmfully, as a function of k. Report a 'self-correction recovery curve' and per-model recovery half-life. Ship the harness.

**Why it matters:** Self-correction capacity is a defensible property (a model that can recover mid-harm is more robust to prefill/multi-turn attacks) and is currently unmeasured. Complements depth metrics with a recovery metric. Inference-only, single GPU, fits 30h.

**Relevant context:** Qi et al. (arXiv:2406.05946): once the initial safeguard is bypassed 'the model often freely generates harmful content' — implying low recovery; this benchmark quantifies recovery directly. Crescendo (arXiv:2404.01833) exploits the same momentum effect.

title: Persuasion-Triggered Sycophancy as an Oversight Failure Probe

original_idea.body:
# Persuasion-Triggered Sycophancy as an Oversight Failure Probe

**Problem:** Measuring Opinion Bias and Sycophancy via LLM-based Persuasion (arXiv:2604.21564, Apr 2026) finds argumentative debate is a far stronger sycophancy trigger than direct opinion-asking (up to 94%). This implies debate-based oversight could systematically corrupt the judge — but the link to verdict accuracy on factual tasks is untested.

**Direction:** Use a factual QA set with known answers. Have a 'persuader' model argue for a wrong answer to the judge and measure how often the judge abandons a correct initial verdict. Compare direct-ask vs. argumentative framings to replicate the 94% gap and quantify the resulting accuracy loss specifically in an oversight (judge) role.

# Pressure-Response Curve for CoT Obfuscation Under Increasing Stealth Demands

**Problem:** Models can obfuscate their CoT under 'high pressure' (monitors then catch only ~10% of deception), but the relationship between the strength of the stealth instruction and the resulting monitor evasion is treated as binary (low vs high) rather than as a continuous dose-response curve.

**Direction:** Construct a graded ladder of stealth-pressure prompts (from 'just do the task' to 'hide your true intent from any reader at all costs') and have a small open reasoning model perform a benign-with-side-goal task at each level. Measure monitor catch-rate at each pressure level, producing a continuous obfuscation pressure-response curve and identifying the pressure threshold where monitorability collapses.

**Why it matters:** Tells us how much adversarial pressure CoT monitoring can absorb before failing, informing whether CoT monitoring is a robust or brittle line of defense. The graded design is novel relative to the binary framings in the literature and needs no training.

**Relevant context:** Can Reasoning Models Obfuscate Reasoning? (arxiv 2510.19851): CoT monitoring effective without obfuscation pressure but high-pressure obfuscation defeats it, monitors catch ~10% under high pressure; models hide intent with vague internal language and benign external text. # Defer-to-Resample Threshold Tuning Without a Real Untrusted Model

**Problem:** The Ctrl-Z resampling protocol (defer-to-resample beats defer-to-trusted: 83% vs 73% safety at 95% usefulness) was validated in a specific agentic setting. Practitioners lack intuition for how its safety-usefulness frontier shifts with the deferral threshold and number of resamples in a simpler, reproducible toy setting.

**Direction:** Build a minimal simulated control game: a small open model occasionally inserts a 'backdoor' token, a monitor scores suspiciousness, and a resampling protocol re-queries up to n times choosing the least-suspicious action. **Why it matters:** Gives a teachable, fully open re-implementation of a key control protocol, letting small researchers reason about parameter choices. Reproducing the headline result on accessible models confirms its generality and builds reusable infrastructure.

**Relevant context:** Ctrl-Z: Controlling AI Agents via Resampling (arxiv 2504.10374): defer-to-trusted gives 72.7% safety at 95% usefulness; defer-to-resample gives 83.2%; resampling re-queries the untrusted model n times and selects the minimum-suspiciousness action below threshold, else defers to trusted.

# Linear Deception Probes: Do They Survive a Distribution Shift to Agentic Sabotage?

**Problem:** Apollo's linear deception probes hit AUROC 0.96-0.999 on their evaluation datasets, but probes are known to over-fit their training distribution. title: Distributed-Threat Aggregation: Catching Sabotage That No Single Action Reveals

original_idea.body:
# Distributed-Threat Aggregation: Catching Sabotage That No Single Action Reveals

**Problem:** Diffuse threats (research sabotage via many individually-innocuous bad actions) need fundamentally different monitoring than concentrated threats, yet most control evals focus on catching a single incriminating action. There is little public tooling for the aggregation problem: combining many weak per-action signals into a population-level alarm.

**Direction:** Simulate a stream of agent actions where a small fraction are subtly degraded (e.g. quietly worse code, omitted edge cases) so that each action alone is near-undetectable. Apply simple statistical aggregation (sequential probability ratio test, CUSUM, running mean of monitor scores) and measure how many actions are needed to raise a reliable alarm at a fixed false-alarm rate.

**Why it matters:** Diffuse research-sabotage is a medium-horizon threat frontier labs deprioritize, and the aggregation-over-many-actions framing is under-tooled. A simple, statistics-based detector is squarely within the participant's skill set and is counterfactually valuable lab-independent infrastructure.

**Relevant context:** Redwood 'How can we solve diffuse threats like research sabotage with AI control?': distinguishes diffuse threats (catastrophe needs many weak-evidence actions) from concentrated threats (few highly incriminating actions); different monitoring approaches needed. UK AISI lists detecting concentrated vs distributed failures as an open problem.

title: Evaluation-Awareness Probe: Can Small Models Tell They Are Being Tested?

original_idea.body:
# Evaluation-Awareness Probe: Can Small Models Tell They Are Being Tested?

**Problem:** Evaluation awareness scales with model size and undermines the validity of all safety evals, but most evidence is on frontier models. Whether and how small open models discriminate 'this is a test' from 'this is real deployment' contexts is poorly characterized at the small end where hobbyists can experiment.

**Direction:** Construct matched prompt pairs that are semantically identical but stylistically signal 'benchmark/eval' vs 'real user' framing. Ask small open models to classify which context they are in, and separately measure whether their behavior on a benign task shifts between framings. Plot evaluation-awareness accuracy across a size ladder of small open models.

**Why it matters:** If even small models detect eval framing, honeypot and control evaluations need careful camouflage. Mapping where awareness emerges across the accessible size range is a clean, reproducible study that frontier labs cannot easily publish on open models.

**Relevant context:** Sandbagging/eval-awareness literature: evaluation awareness follows a power-law with model size, worsening each frontier generation (kili-technology Muse Spark analysis; sandbagging detection survey). Honeypot Protocol relies on models not detecting the evaluation condition (arxiv 2604.13301).
